preserve: Decision under consideration: increase the Pro price from £49 to £59 with the next Pro feature release.
Comparator: keep the Pro price at £49.
Current skeleton factors: Pro price, feature release, Pro subscriber count, and monthly churn.
Core uncertainty: the price increase's effects on churn, subscriber growth, and the feature release's effect on growth.

proposed_options.label: Raise Pro to £59 for new subscribers at the feature release, while grandfathering existing Pro subscribers for a defined period or until a renewal event.
proposed_options.why_material: This separates acquisition-price elasticity from immediate exposure of the existing base, potentially reducing near-term cancellation risk while still testing the higher price point.

proposed_options.label: Run a staged or segmented £59 price test around the feature release before making £59 the default price.
proposed_options.why_material: A controlled rollout can produce evidence on conversion, downgrades, cancellations, and net MRR before broad exposure creates a churn breach.

proposed_options.label: Keep Pro at £49 and monetize the released capability through an optional add-on or a higher plan tier.
proposed_options.why_material: This creates an alternative route to higher revenue that may preserve the perceived value of the existing Pro plan for price-sensitive customers.

proposed_factors.label: New-customer conversion to Pro at each price point
proposed_factors.why_material: A higher list price can change the rate at which prospective customers become Pro subscribers, affecting subscriber growth and MRR.

proposed_factors.label: Existing-customer cancellation and downgrade behavior at renewal
proposed_factors.why_material: A price change may lead customers either to cancel or move to a lower plan; these pathways have different implications for logo churn, subscriber count, and MRR.

proposed_factors.label: Perceived value of the feature release relative to the £59 price
proposed_factors.why_material: Customers' assessment of whether the release justifies the price is a plausible mediator of both purchase conversion and retention.

proposed_factors.label: Feature adoption and realized customer benefit
proposed_factors.why_material: Merely releasing a feature need not improve retention; adoption and realized benefit are more defensible mechanisms through which it could affect willingness to pay and churn.

proposed_factors.label: Gross Pro additions and net Pro subscriber growth
proposed_factors.why_material: MRR progress depends on additions as well as retention; net subscriber growth makes the trade-off between higher ARPU and lower conversion or retention visible.

proposed_factors.label: Definition and cohorting of monthly churn
proposed_factors.why_material: The decision needs clarity on whether the under-4% constraint is customer/logo churn or revenue churn, and whether it is measured for exposed renewal cohorts versus the blended base.

proposed_risks.label: The feature release does not create enough perceived or realized value to offset price sensitivity.
proposed_risks.why_material: If the value proposition is unclear or the feature is not adopted, the joint release-and-price-change may weaken conversion and retention rather than support them.

proposed_risks.label: Downgrades may reduce MRR without necessarily appearing as customer churn.
proposed_risks.why_material: A customer who remains subscribed on a lower plan may leave logo churn below 4% while still undermining MRR progress.

proposed_risks.label: A blended churn metric may mask a harmful response among customers exposed to the increase.
proposed_risks.why_material: Unexposed customers or new cohorts can dilute the aggregate metric, delaying detection of price-change-related retention problems.

proposed_risks.label: Grandfathering or segmentation may create pricing complexity or perceived unfairness.
proposed_risks.why_material: A risk-mitigating rollout can itself affect customer trust, support burden, and eventual migration to the new price.

proposed_outcomes.label: Net MRR change from the price-and-release decision
proposed_outcomes.why_material: The relevant revenue outcome combines the higher price paid by retained subscribers with changes in conversions, additions, downgrades, and cancellations.

proposed_outcomes.label: Monthly churn among customers exposed to the new price
proposed_outcomes.why_material: This outcome directly tests whether the decision is compatible with the churn constraint, rather than relying only on a blended churn result.

proposed_outcomes.label: Revenue per retained Pro subscriber
proposed_outcomes.why_material: This distinguishes the benefit of a higher price from changes in the size of the Pro subscriber base.

proposed_links.to: Perceived value of the feature release relative to the £59 price
proposed_links.why_material: Holding perceived product value constant, a higher price can reduce customers' assessment of price-value fit; the feature release may counteract this through increased perceived value.

proposed_links.from: Feature adoption and realized customer benefit
proposed_links.to: Perceived value of the feature release relative to the £59 price
proposed_links.why_material: Customers who adopt the release and obtain meaningful benefit may perceive stronger value at the new price.

proposed_links.from: Perceived value of the feature release relative to the £59 price
proposed_links.to: New-customer conversion to Pro at each price point
proposed_links.why_material: Stronger perceived value can support willingness to purchase Pro, whereas weak price-value fit can suppress conversion.

proposed_links.from: Perceived value of the feature release relative to the £59 price
proposed_links.to: Existing-customer cancellation and downgrade behavior at renewal
proposed_links.why_material: Stronger perceived value can reduce the propensity to cancel or downgrade at renewal after a price change.

proposed_links.from: Existing-customer cancellation and downgrade behavior at renewal
proposed_links.why_material: More cancellations among eligible customers increase churn; downgrades may not increase logo churn and should therefore be tracked separately.

proposed_links.from: New-customer conversion to Pro at each price point
proposed_links.to: Gross Pro additions and net Pro subscriber growth
proposed_links.why_material: Higher conversion among qualified prospects contributes to gross additions and, all else equal, net subscriber growth.

proposed_links.from: Existing-customer cancellation and downgrade behavior at renewal
proposed_links.to: Gross Pro additions and net Pro subscriber growth
proposed_links.why_material: Cancellations and plan exits reduce the active Pro base, while downgrades can remove customers from Pro even if they remain customers.

proposed_links.from: Gross Pro additions and net Pro subscriber growth
proposed_links.to: Net MRR change from the price-and-release decision
proposed_links.why_material: More net active Pro subscribers increases recurring revenue, conditional on the revenue associated with each subscriber.
For retained customers actually charged the new price, a higher Pro price increases recurring revenue per subscriber before discounts, grandfathering, or plan changes.

proposed_links.to: Net MRR change from the price-and-release decision
proposed_links.why_material: Higher recurring revenue per retained subscriber contributes to net MRR, but does not by itself establish that total MRR rises because subscriber counts may also change.

excluded.candidate: Assuming that the £59 price increase will increase total MRR.
excluded.reason: Higher price per retained subscriber can be offset by lower conversion, downgrades, or cancellations; no evidence for the net effect was provided.

excluded.candidate: Assuming that the feature release will increase the number of Pro subscribers.
excluded.reason: The release's value, adoption, and effect on purchase and retention were not specified.

excluded.candidate: Assuming a specific customer segment, competitive benchmark, or willingness-to-pay level.
excluded.reason: The brief supplies no segmentation, market, or customer-research evidence.

fidelity_warnings: The skeleton's direct link from Pro plan price to MRR is directionally incomplete: price affects MRR through revenue per paying subscriber and through changes in acquisition, retention, and plan mix.

The skeleton's direct link from monthly churn rate to MRR compresses an important mechanism. Churn reduces retained subscribers (and potentially retained recurring revenue), which then affects MRR; the impact also depends on gross additions and pricing.

The asserted positive link from the feature release to number of Pro subscribers is not established by the brief. A more defensible causal path runs through feature adoption, realized benefit, perceived value, conversion, and retention.
The churn constraint is underspecified: customer/logo churn and revenue churn can move differently, especially if customers downgrade instead of canceling.

The goal wording says 'reaching £20k MRR within 12 months,' while the skeleton expresses an end-horizon threshold; it does not clarify whether attaining the threshold at any point, sustaining it, or ending month 12 at or above it is intended.
